header: IN THE PESHAWAR HIGH COURT, PESHAWAR
body: Date of hearing……………….24.11.2026…………………………... Appellant (Abdul Haleem) By Mr. Shabbir Hussain Gigyani, Advocate. Respondents. (State) By Mr. Abdul Qayyum Khattak, AAG and (Complainant) By M/s. Sohail Akhtar, Hussain Ali and Sajid Khan (On Video Link), Advocates.

******************* MUHAMMAD FAHEEM WALI, J.- Through this common judgment, I intend to decide Criminal Appeals No.1038-P/2025 and 1004- P/2025, both instituted by Abdul Haleem (convict), as well as Criminal Revision No.243- P/2025, filed by Ubaid-ur-Rehman (complainant), as all these proceedings arise out of one and the same judgment passed by the learned Additional District and Sessions Judge / Sessions Judge, Lahor, Swabi, whereby the appeal preferred by the convict against his conviction and sentence was dismissed, whereas the revision petition filed by the complainant, seeking enhancement of the sentence, was allowed.

2. Briefly stated, the facts giving rise to the instant proceedings are that on 09.09.2024, the complainant, Ubaid-ur-Rehman, while lying in injured condition in the casualty department of BKMC, Shah Mansoor, Swabi, reported to the local police that on the same day, at 09:00 AM, he was standing in front of his house along with his brother, Abdul Lateef, and his father, Abdur Rauf, when the accused, Abdul Haleem, duly armed, arrived at the spot and opened fire at him with the intention of committing his Qatl-i-Amd, as a result whereof he sustained serious injuries. The motive behind the occurrence was stated to be a dispute over landed property. Upon completion of investigation, the challan was submitted before the learned Judicial Magistrate, who, after conducting the trial and recording the evidence of the prosecution witnesses, convicted the accused under Sections 324, 337-D and 337-F(vi) PPC vide judgment dated 22.07.2025 and sentenced him as follows: under Section 324 PPC, to imprisonment for two years along with a fine of Rs.10,000/-, or in default thereof, to undergo one month’s simple imprisonment; under Section 337- D PPC, to pay one-third of the Diyat, amounting to Rs.27,01,318/-, as Arsh; and under Section 337- F(vi) PPC, to one year’s simple imprisonment along with Daman of Rs.70,000/-. The benefit of Section 382-B Cr.P.C was extended to him, and all the sentences were ordered to run concurrently.

3. Feeling aggrieved, the convict preferred an appeal before the learned Sessions Court, whereas the complainant filed a criminal revision seeking enhancement of the sentences awarded by the learned trial Court. The learned Sessions Judge, after hearing learned counsel for the parties and examining the evidence available on record, dismissed the appeal of the convict and accepted the revision of the complainant. Consequently, the sentence under Section 324 PPC was enhanced from two years to five years’ simple imprisonment; the sentence under Section 337- F(vi) PPC was enhanced from one year to three years’ simple imprisonment; and an additional sentence of three years’ simple imprisonment was awarded under Section 337-D PPC, while the respective financial liabilities by way of Arsh and Daman were maintained. The benefit of Section 382-B Cr.P.C and the direction regarding concurrent running of the sentences were also kept intact. Dissatisfied with the said decision, the convict has instituted the above-mentioned appeals before this Court, whereas the complainant has filed the connected criminal revision seeking further enhancement of the sentences.
4. I have heard the arguments of learned counsel for the parties as well as the learned Assistant Advocate General and have gone through the record with their valuable assistance.

5. Before adverting to the merits of the controversy, it would be appropriate to first determine the competence and maintainability of the proceedings instituted before this Court, particularly when the convict has approached this Court through appeals against a judgment rendered by the learned Sessions Judge in the exercise of both appellate and revisional jurisdictions, while the complainant has invoked the revisional jurisdiction of this Court against an order passed by the learned Sessions Judge in exercise of powers under Section 439-A Cr.P.C. The question of maintainability goes to the very root of the jurisdiction of this Court and, therefore, has to be answered at the threshold.

6. It is a settled principle that a right of appeal is a creation of statute and does not exist unless it is expressly conferred by law. This principle finds statutory expression in Section 404 Cr.P.C, which provides that no appeal shall lie from any judgment or order of a Criminal Court except as provided for by the Code or by any other law for the time being in force. Admittedly, the original conviction in the present case was recorded by the learned Judicial Magistrate, against which the statutory remedy available to the convict was an appeal before the Court of Session under Section 408 Cr.P.C. The said remedy was duly availed of by him, and his appeal was dismissed by the learned Sessions Judge. Section 410 Cr.P.C, on the other hand, provides a right of appeal to the High Court against a conviction recorded on a trial held by a Sessions Judge or an Additional Sessions Judge. The provision, by its very terms, is confined to the exercise of original criminal jurisdiction by the Court of Session and, therefore, does not confer a right of second appeal against a judgment rendered by the Sessions Judge while exercising appellate jurisdiction under Section 408 Cr.P.C. The distinction between an original trial and an appellate determination is material and cannot be overlooked. The position is further fortified by Section 430 Cr.P.C, which declares that judgments and orders passed by an Appellate Court upon appeal shall be final, except in the cases provided for in Section 417 and Chapter XXXII of the Code. Thus, once the statutory appeal against the conviction recorded by the Magistrate has been availed of before the Court of Session, a further appeal under Section 410 Cr.P.C does not lie to this Court merely because the appellate judgment has been rendered by a Sessions Judge.

7. Nevertheless, the absence of a further statutory appeal does not altogether exclude the supervisory jurisdiction of this Court over an appellate judgment rendered by the Sessions Judge. The finality attached to such a judgment by Section 430 Cr.P.C is itself expressly made subject to Chapter XXXII of the Code, which comprises, inter alia, Sections 435 and 439 Cr.P.C. The revisional jurisdiction of this Court, therefore, remains available against such a judgment, subject, of course, to the restrictions expressly imposed by Section 439 Cr.P.C itself. In this regard, guidance may be sought from the judgment of the learned Sindh High Court reported as Jeendal Shah v. The State (2025 MLD 1019), wherein, after examining the relevant provisions of the Code, it was clarified that no second appeal lies before the High Court against a judgment passed by the Sessions Court in its appellate jurisdiction under Section 408 Cr.P.C, and that the aggrieved person may, instead, invoke the revisional jurisdiction of the High Court under Section 439 Cr.P.C, subject to the conditions prescribed by law.

8. In view of the foregoing legal position, the two appeals bearing No.1038-P/2025 and 1004-P/2025, notwithstanding their nomenclature, are treated as and converted into criminal revisions under Section 439 Cr.P.C insofar as they call in question the decision rendered by the learned Sessions Judge in his appellate jurisdiction. The mere misdescription of a proceeding would not, by itself, defeat the substance of the remedy where the Court otherwise possesses jurisdiction to entertain the matter in its appropriate legal form. It is by now well settled that the mentioning of a wrong or inapplicable provision of law, or the non-mentioning of the applicable one, while invoking a jurisdiction which is otherwise vested in a Court, does not by itself entail fatal consequences, as held by the Supreme Court of Pakistan in Sultan Ahmed v. Registrar, Balochistan High Court, Quetta and others (2023 SCMR 1955). Likewise, in Noman Mansoor alias Nomi v. The State (PLD 2024 Supreme Court 805), the Supreme Court upheld the conversion of a criminal appeal into a criminal revision by the High Court, observing that under Section 439 Cr.P.C the High Court may, in its discretion, exercise any of the powers conferred on a Court of appeal. The conversion is, thus, a matter of form and not of substance; what matters is the jurisdiction which the Court in fact exercises and the limits within which it is to be exercised.

9. However, a separate statutory restriction governs the revisional jurisdiction of this Court in respect of an order passed by the Sessions Judge while exercising powers under Section 439-A Cr.P.C. Clause (b) of sub-section (4) of Section 439 Cr.P.C expressly provides that nothing in that section shall be deemed to authorise a High Court to entertain any proceedings in revision with respect to an order made by the Sessions Judge under Section 439-A Cr.P.C. The prohibition is categorical and admits of no exception in the ordinary exercise of revisional jurisdiction. Its evident object is to prevent a multiplicity of revisional proceedings. The Code confers revisional jurisdiction over the orders of Magistrates both upon the Sessions Judge and upon this Court; but once an aggrieved party elects to approach the Sessions Judge and an order is passed thereon under Section 439-A Cr.P.C, a second revision against that order is barred. It has consistently been held that such a second revision is not competent and that the bar cannot be circumvented merely by giving the proceedings a different label; reference in this regard may be made to The State v. Ch. Altaf Hussain and 2 others (PLD 1978 Lahore 1259); Muhammad Afzal v. Aminul Haq and another (1982 P.Cr.L.J 340); Sarwar Ali v. The State (1983 P.Cr.L.J 329); and Abdul Hayee and others v. Muhammad Shafiq and others (PLD 1986 Lahore 165). Consequently, the portion of the impugned judgment whereby the learned Sessions Judge accepted the complainant’s revision and enhanced the sentences, having been rendered in exercise of revisional jurisdiction under Section 439-A Cr.P.C, cannot be subjected to another round of revision before this Court under Section 439 Cr.P.C. The same statutory restriction operates against either party, irrespective of whether the challenge is brought by the convict seeking reduction or setting aside of the enhanced sentences, or by the complainant seeking their further enhancement.

10. Thus, the complainant, having already availed of the remedy of revision before the learned Sessions Judge under Section 439-A Cr.P.C, cannot maintain another revision before this Court against the order passed by that Court in exercise of the said jurisdiction. Accordingly, Criminal Revision No.243-P/2025, instituted by Ubaid-ur-Rehman, is incompetent and not maintainable in view of the express bar contained in Section 439(4)(b) Cr.P.C. Likewise, the challenge of the convict to the revisional portion of the impugned judgment also falls beyond the scope of the revisional jurisdiction conferred upon this Court by Section 439 Cr.P.C. The two converted criminal revisions, however, remain examinable to the extent that they assail the decision rendered by the learned Sessions Judge in his appellate jurisdiction.

11. Coming to the merits of the convict’s challenge to the appellate decision, it must be borne in mind that the scope of revisional jurisdiction is narrower than that of appellate jurisdiction. Revisional jurisdiction is, in essence, supervisory and corrective in nature; as envisaged by Section 435 Cr.P.C, its object is to enable this Court to satisfy itself as to the correctness, legality or propriety of any finding, sentence or order of the Court below, and as to the regularity of its proceedings. This Court is, therefore, not expected to undertake a fresh appraisal of the entire evidence merely because another view may be possible, more so where the findings of guilt are concurrent. Interference is warranted only where the impugned findings suffer from illegality, material irregularity, jurisdictional defect or perversity, or are the result of patent misreading or non-reading of evidence occasioning a miscarriage of justice. Tested on this touchstone, a perusal of the impugned judgment reveals that the learned Sessions Judge examined the prosecution evidence in detail and recorded specific reasons for maintaining the conviction of the accused.

12. The prosecution case primarily rests upon the statement of the injured complainant, Ubaid-ur-Rehman (PW-8), who is also an eyewitness of the occurrence, and that of Abdur Rauf (PW-9), another eyewitness. Their statements were found consistent on material particulars and remained unshaken during crossexamination. The ocular account received corroboration from the medical evidence furnished by the Medical Officer (PW-3), who confirmed the firearm injuries sustained by the complainant and their classification under the relevant provisions of the Pakistan Penal Code. The Investigating Officer (PW-11) also deposed regarding the recoveries effected during investigation, including the crime empties, bloodstained earth, blood-stained garments and the crime weapon. The forensic examination further supported the prosecution case, inasmuch as the crime empties were found to have been fired from the recovered firearm, while the forensic reports concerning the blood-stained articles also furnished corroborative evidence.

13. The learned Sessions Judge, after considering the ocular account, the medical evidence, the recoveries and the forensic reports in their entirety, found that the prosecution had established the charge against the convict beyond reasonable doubt. Learned counsel for the convict has not been able to point out any material contradiction or discrepancy which could reasonably impair the credibility of the injured eyewitness or of the other prosecution evidence. The defence version was also duly considered by the Courts below, but no convincing material was brought on record to substantiate the same. The mere denial of the allegations by the accused in his statement recorded under Section 342 Cr.P.C, unsupported by any material, was rightly not considered sufficient to discredit the otherwise confidence-inspiring prosecution evidence.

14. It is well settled that the testimony of an injured witness ordinarily carries considerable evidentiary value, as his presence at the place of occurrence stands established by the injuries sustained by him, and it is seldom that such a witness would let the real culprit go and falsely implicate an innocent person in his place. Nevertheless, the stamp of injury, by itself, establishes presence and not truthfulness; the testimony of an injured witness is, therefore, to be assessed on its own merits and in conjunction with the remaining evidence on record. In the present case, the statement of the injured complainant does not stand in isolation; rather, it is supported by the account of another eyewitness of the occurrence and by the medical and forensic evidence. The learned Sessions Judge, therefore, committed no illegality in placing reliance upon the prosecution evidence and maintaining the conviction of the accused under the relevant provisions of law.

15. The conviction under Section 324 PPC is also borne out by the circumstances of the occurrence. Section 324 PPC is attracted where a person does any act with such intention or knowledge, and under such circumstances, that, if he by that act caused qatl, he would be guilty of qatl-i-amd. Such intention, being a state of mind, is seldom capable of direct proof and has ordinarily to be gathered from the attending circumstances, such as the nature of the weapon employed, the manner in which the attack was launched, and the nature and seat of the injuries caused. In the present case, the use of a firearm, the manner in which the complainant was attacked and the injuries sustained by him, as appreciated by the Courts below, sufficiently establish the requisite intention and conduct attracting the said provision. Similarly, the medical evidence was found sufficient to substantiate the hurt offences under Sections 337-D and 337-F(vi) PPC. No material misreading or non-reading of evidence, nor any other jurisdictional defect in the appellate determination of the conviction, has been demonstrated before this Court.

16. So far as Criminal Appeal No.1004- P/2025, filed by the appellant Abdul Haleem against his conviction and sentence under Section 15 of the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Arms Act, 2013, is concerned, it transpires from the record that the appellant was apprehended in possession of a 30bore pistol (without number) along with a fixed charger containing three (03) live rounds. The prosecution, by producing cogent, reliable and confidence-inspiring evidence, has successfully established the charge against him. Learned counsel for the appellant has also failed to point out any material illegality, misreading or nonreading of evidence, or any other infirmity warranting interference by this Court in its revisional jurisdiction. Consequently, this converted criminal revision, being devoid of merit, is hereby dismissed.

17. For what has been discussed above, both Criminal Appeals No.1038-P/2025 and 1004- P/2025 are converted into criminal revisions under Section 439 Cr.P.C and, to the extent of their challenge to the appellate judgment maintaining the conviction of Abdul Haleem, are dismissed. The challenge to the portion of the impugned judgment passed by the learned Sessions Judge in exercise of revisional jurisdiction under Section 439-A Cr.P.C is not entertainable before this Court in view of the express prohibition contained in Section 439(4)(b) Cr.P.C. Criminal Revision No.243-P/2025, filed by Ubaid-ur-Rehman, is also dismissed, being incompetent and not maintainable under the said statutory provision. Needless to mention that, since Abdul Haleem, the appellant/petitioner, who is on bail, is present before the Court, he be taken into custody and sent to the judicial lock-up to serve out the sentences awarded to him. These are the detailed reasons for the short order of even date delivered in Cr.Appeal No.1038-P/2025.
Announced:
J U D G E /*Saif. SCS*/ (SB) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Muhammad Faheem Wali, J.
